visits.text: The best place to start in Arica is Morro de Arica, the coffee-colored rock overlooking the port. On June 7, 1880, Chilean troops stormed it during the War of the Pacific; the Museo Histórico y de Armas tells the story of the battle at the summit, near the Cristo de la Concordia and an enormous Chilean flag. Head up in the late afternoon: the view over the city and the bay rewards the climb.

Thirty-two Chinchorro mummies still lie in the sand where they were found, beneath the floor of the Museo de Sitio Colón 10. Their discovery was a stroke of luck: an architect had bought the house to turn it into a hotel. Several children still wear mud masks painted red. The audio guide is included; finish on the covered terrace overlooking the city.

Gothic in appearance, but made of metal: the Catedral de San Marcos came from Gustave Eiffel’s workshops. The entire structure is metal; only the doors are wooden. It replaced the former main church, which had been destroyed, and has been listed as a national monument since 1984. It stands beside Plaza Colón, at the foot of the Morro. Continue to the Ex-Aduana, a few streets away.

You will next pass by the Ex-Aduana de Arica, the former customs house, also designed by Eiffel. Its components were prefabricated in Paris and assembled on-site in 1874. The train station is next door, and the Casa de la Gobernación, inaugurated in 1907, rounds out this short Eiffel circuit downtown. You can cover it all on foot in about 1 hour.

activities.text: Warm sand, thick air, calm water: after the Altiplano, Playa Chinchorro feels like a return to earth. Its tranquil waters and nearby amenities make it the family beach of Arica, nicknamed the city of eternal spring. Allow about three hours for the descent from Putre and save the afternoon for the beach.

You can also try El Laucho and La Lisera, two other popular beaches in Arica. The sun shines here almost all year. Keep the evening low-key: the next day’s drive south to the Atacama Giant covers more than 250 km.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert
Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Parque El Loa, in southern Calama, lines the Río Loa with lawns, trees, and pools, a true green oasis in the desert. It features a replica of the church in Chiu Chiu, built in 1985 to bring the culture of the Upper Loa closer to the city. Admission is free; it’s an ideal break after the drive.

In the copper capital, even the cathedral is covered in it: Catedral San Juan Bautista, on Plaza 23 de Marzo, has a copper roof donated by Codelco. A visit is free and quick, taking 20 to 30 minutes. Aeropuerto El Loa is about 6 km southeast of downtown.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert
Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Casablanca Valley didn't exist viticulturally before 1982: Pablo Morandé was the first to bet on this terrain of fog and wind 25 km from the Pacific, where everyone saw only a humid desert. He was right. Today, 6,000 hectares almost exclusively in whites and Pinot Noir. The contrast with Maipo is immediate: temperatures here are sometimes 10°C lower than Santiago on the same day. It's the Humboldt Current effect—cold Pacific air rushes into the valleys each afternoon.

Casas del Bosque, founded in 1993, is one of the valley's most pedagogically readable wineries—well-structured tour, trained guides, and the Tanino restaurant on the terrace offers direct vineyard views. The 'Pequeñas Producciones Pinot Noir' is the cuvée to request absolutely: this is where Casablanca shows its best, in these fresh, tense reds nobody expected from Chile.

Technically in the San Antonio Valley (Rosario subzone; plan a round trip from Casablanca), Matetic is worth extending the drive. Founded in 1999 and certified organic and biodynamic as early as 2002, the estate may be the most architecturally beautiful in South America: wood and concrete sculpted by architect Laurence Odfjell, a gravity-flow cellar where grapes descend simply by gravity without pumping. The EQ Syrah cuvée—peppery and mineral notes—is one of the continent's great Syrahs. Tour + tasting $40-50.

activities.text: Comparative tasting Sauvignon Blanc vs Chardonnay from Casablanca at Casas del Bosque or during the Matetic visit: this is the day's central exercise. Casablanca Sauvignon Blanc has the citrus and tension of cool-climate terroir, Chardonnay the roundness and substance. Both are radically different from their Burgundian or New Zealand equivalents. Take notes.

Spend the night in the valley if possible - La Casona at Matetic is the most immersive option. Alternatively, continue to Valparaíso, about 40 km from Casablanca, a 35-minute drive, for the night and enjoy the city the following morning in the best conditions.

days_plan.itin_title: 8-Day Wine Route Through Chile: Maipo, Casablanca & Colchagua

activities.text: A giant dune right beside a city: Cerro Dragón towers over Iquique and is visible from almost everywhere. People come here for sandboarding, riding a board down the sand. Go through a local operator that provides equipment, and avoid the middle of the day, when the sun beats down on the sand.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

places.name: Chiu Chiu

visits.text: Completed around the middle of the 17th century, the Iglesia de San Francisco de Chiu Chiu is considered Chile’s oldest church. With adobe walls, a cactus-wood ceiling, and priests’ graves in the courtyard, it has been a national monument since 1951. The feast of San Francisco takes place here every October 4.

“Atacama la Chica” is the name the Spanish gave Chiu Chiu when they founded the present-day village. It sits at 2,525 m, near the confluence of the Loa and Salado rivers, about thirty kilometers from Calama. Stop at the square for lunch before heading to San Pedro de Atacama.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

map_keywords: San Francisco de Chiu Chiu Church

activities.text: If tours are available during your stay, the Chuquicamata mine, operated by Codelco 16 km north of Calama, is impressive in scale: it is one of the world’s largest open-pit copper mines. The free guided tour lasts about three hours and passes through the former mining settlement, abandoned to make way for mining operations. Check with Codelco and book before your trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

activities.text: Jagged cliffs, a rocky coast and crashing waves: about ten kilometers south of the center, the quiet beaches give way to the Cuevas de Anzota. The Chinchorro already occupied these caves beside the Pacific. Access to the area is closed as a precaution because of falling rocks. Do not plan the coastal walk until the authorities have announced its reopening.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

places.name: El Tatio

visits.text: Columns of steam in below-freezing temperatures: at sunrise, the Géiseres del Tatio, at 4,320 m, are at their best, when the temperature difference makes the plumes more visible. This is the world’s third-largest geyser field and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere. Dress in layers: in winter, temperatures can reach -15°C at dawn.

The field is vast, but the jets are modest: at El Tatio, they rise to an average height of just 75 cm. The name could mean “oven” or “grandfather”; etymologies differ. Stay behind the stones marking the vents, as the water emerges boiling hot.

activities.text: You will leave San Pedro de Atacama around 5 a.m. to arrive at El Tatio between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m., taking the B-245, a gravel track approximately 80 km long. On the return trip in daylight, watch for wild vicuñas grazing in the high-altitude wetlands around the site. Admission is paid on arrival, with no reservation required.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

map_keywords: El Tatio San Pedro de Atacama

visits.text: Around a hundred stone llamas walk toward the sea: the Tiliviche Geoglyphs cover the southern slope of the ravine, about 600 m west of the Pan-American Highway. They may have marked a caravan route to the coast; others see them as part of a ritual. Archaeologist Luis Briones’s team restored them in the 1980s. View them from the northern slope, where they are clearly visible.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: At 86 m, the Atacama Giant is the largest known prehistoric depiction of a human figure, lying on the western slope of Cerro Unita, 15 km from Huara. Who created it is unknown, and estimates of its age vary; it may depict an Andean deity. The last kilometer of the access road is unpaved, and you must not climb the hill.

The giant draws every eye, but it is not alone: Cerro Unita has around twenty other geometric and animal figures on its western and southern slopes. Vehicle tracks have already caused lasting damage to the site. Stay in the viewing area at the foot of the hill.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Mint-green walls and Douglas fir woodwork: Humberstone’s theater once welcomed any worker who could afford a ticket. The town had more than 3,700 residents before it closed around 1960. Buy your ticket here; it also covers Santa Laura.

Humberstone’s most astonishing feature is a riveted iron swimming pool, complete with a diving board, in the middle of the Atacama Desert. Empty today, it recalls the social life of this workers’ town. Bring a hat and sunscreen; shade is scarce between the buildings.

Saltpeter workers were paid in tokens they could spend in company stores. In December 1907, their campaign for better conditions ended in a massacre at a school in Iquique, and a small room in Humberstone is dedicated to it. Take the time to read the information panels.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: You’ll start at Plaza Arturo Prat, the heart of Iquique, and its Torre del Reloj, donated by the city’s English community. Its three progressively narrower stories serve as a landmark throughout the historic center. The square is freely accessible day and night. Teatro Municipal stands on one side, making it easy to continue there without a detour.

Built in 1890, when saltpeter was making Iquique wealthy, Teatro Municipal has four female figures on its facade representing the seasons. A national monument since 1977, it has hosted European operas as well as local events. To take in the entire facade, step back into the square before approaching.

Cobblestones and grand wooden houses give Paseo Baquedano the feel of a street in a Western. Its late-19th-century homes were paid for by the “white gold” of saltpeter. At number 951, Museo Regional occupies a house dating from 1892. Walk along the street from Plaza Prat, preferably late in the day for the light.

Nothing captures the luxury of the saltpeter barons quite like Palacio Astoreca. Juan Higinio Astoreca, who owned several saltpeter works, had it built in 1904 entirely from pine wood. Now a cultural center, it is open for interior visits. Check the hours before coming.

A replica, but full-size: Museo Corbeta Esmeralda recreates the Chilean corvette sunk during the naval Battle of Iquique on May 21, 1879. You can board it to relive a major episode of the War of the Pacific, and a buoy still marks the wreck’s location. Combine your visit with nearby Caleta Riquelme, a fishing harbor and fish market.

activities.text: Playa Cavancha, Iquique’s main beach, stretches along the edge of downtown with its golden sand. Paseo Costanera continues along the shore for 4 km, from Bellavista to Huantajaya. In the morning, calmer seas are suitable for kayaking and paddleboarding around the Cavancha peninsula. For surfing and bodyboarding, head instead to Playa Huayquique, farther south.

If you’ve never flown, Iquique is the place to try paragliding: take off from Alto Hospicio, fly over Cerro Dragón, and land on the beach. A tandem flight with a pilot lasts 10 to 15 minutes. Prices recorded in 2023 ranged from around 60,000 to 90,000 pesos; compare operators and book the day before.

You can finish at Zofri, Iquique’s duty-free zone, home to the city’s largest shopping mall. This is the place to pick up any gear you still need before heading to the Atacama highlands: warm clothes, sunglasses, and sunscreen. Allow some time; the site is vast.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: At an elevation of 4,517 m, Lake Chungará is among the highest lakes in the world. It formed when the Parinacota volcano collapsed and its debris dammed the former Lauca River. In calm weather, the volcano’s cone is reflected in the water. Aim for the morning to see the reflection, and do not stay too long if you feel dizzy.

Residents of the Altiplano, on both the Chilean and Bolivian sides, see deities in the Nevados de Payachata, the twin volcanoes Parinacota and Pomerape that tower over Lake Chungará. Parinacota rises above 6,300 m. Route CH-11 follows the lake’s southern and western shores, making photo stops easy.

activities.text: With binoculars, Lake Chungará becomes a wildlife lookout: giant coots, three species of flamingos, rheas known as suris, and vicuñas live in Parque Nacional Lauca, established in 1970. Above 4,500 m, walk slowly, drink plenty of water, and descend at the first sign of a persistent headache.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: A jagged salt crust stretching as far as the eye can see, a strong smell, then water and pink: Laguna Chaxa appears in the middle of the Salar de Atacama, about 25 km southwest of Toconao. It is part of the Soncor sector of the Reserva Nacional Los Flamencos. The site opens at 8 a.m.

activities.text: Three of the world’s six flamingo species gather at Laguna Chaxa: the Andean, James’s, and Chilean flamingos. According to El Ciudadano, their numbers have declined significantly over roughly fifteen years. Stay on the trails and bring a telephoto lens; the sunsets here are also beautiful.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: The lagoons are separated at the surface by a lava flow but connected underground: Laguna Miñiques, covering 1.6 km² at 4,120 m, is fed by water seeping from neighboring Miscanti. Above it rises the 5,910 m Miñiques volcano. The same ticket covers both lagoons.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

places.name: Laguna Miscanti

visits.text: The most intense blue of the trip awaits at heart-shaped Laguna Miscanti, at over 4,100 m beneath Cerro Miscanti. It is renowned for the contrast between its turquoise water, yellow grass, and surrounding peaks. An admission ticket is required and also covers Miñiques; buy it in advance.

activities.text: If you scan the shores of Laguna Miscanti, you may spot the horned coot, an Altiplano bird that nests here. The road is paved as far as Socaire, then a good track leads to the lagoons, about 115 km from San Pedro de Atacama. Keep your distance from the nests.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

map_keywords: Lagunas Altiplánicas San Pedro de Atacama

visits.text: Matilla is worth a four-kilometer detour from Pica: the Iglesia de San Antonio and its bell tower, a remnant of the original building, overlook this small oasis village founded in the 18th century. Explore on foot; the center is tiny.

Before lemons, there was wine: the Lagar de Matilla, an 18th-century Spanish winepress, recalls the days when the oasis produced wine. The site is small; fifteen minutes is enough before continuing south.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: “Lagoon of the parinas,” meaning flamingos: that is the Aymara meaning of the name Parinacota. Founded in 1625, the hamlet has around thirty residents, with stone and straw houses arranged around the church; it has been designated a zona típica since 1979. Park at the entrance and explore on foot; you can see everything in less than an hour.

Plain outside, striking inside: the Iglesia de Parinacota conceals walls covered in colonial paintings depicting saints and scenes from the Passion. Built in 1670 and rebuilt in 1789, it has been a historic monument since 1979 and is surrounded by a low, whitewashed wall. To see it full of people, aim for the festival of the Virgen de la Natividad in September.

activities.text: You will then cross the Parinacota bofedal, high-altitude wet meadows that retain the little rain that falls on the Altiplano. Vicuñas roam freely here, and the pools attract flamingos and giant coots. Stay on the road and keep your distance: these are wild animals.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Iglesia de San Andrés overlooks the square in Pica, whose official name is San Andrés de Pica. Most of the houses and the church date from the Peruvian period, after 1821. Museo Histórico faces the same square. This is a short visit to make before going for a swim.

Kitschy, but kids love it: Parque de los Dinosaurios, between Pica and Matilla, features a lineup of life-size dinosaur replicas in the oasis. Nothing scientific, just a fun stop popular with families. Half an hour is enough.

activities.text: Water at around 30°C, natural rock, and tropical vegetation: Cocha Resbaladero is a natural pool of moderately warm thermal water in the middle of the desert. “Cocha” comes from Quechua and means a small lagoon. Bring a swimsuit and towel, and preferably come in the morning.

Protected by a designation of origin since 2010, limón de Pica is a small, very tart variety unique to the oasis. Try its juice, along with the mango and guava juices sold in the village. Pick up an alfajor de Pica, made with puff pastry and fruit syrup, for the road.

You can stroll through Pica’s farming area, where mango trees, guava trees, tangelos, and citrus trees grow in the middle of the desert. The contrast between orchards and bare pampa gives the oasis its charm. Stay on the paths and respect the cultivated plots.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: The Lluta Valley marks the start of the ascent to the Altiplano along Route CH-11. On its yellow slopes, you can spot geoglyphs from the car: figures made from stones arranged on the hillside. The valley floor remains green and cultivated, in sharp contrast to the desert. Pull over on a clear stretch of shoulder for photos: farther up, the road becomes winding.

activities.text: If your stay falls on the right day, board the Ferrocarril Arica-Poconchile. It is a slow and different way to leave the city and head inland. Check the operating date and book before you arrive, as the schedule can change.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Flight Calama → Santiago → Temuco (connection). From Temuco, a 112 km drive to Pucón (about 1 hour 30 minutes). The road crosses the Araucanía countryside, historic territory of the Mapuche people, between fields and pine forests. Arrival in Pucón, a town of 20,000 inhabitants on the shores of Lake Villarrica, dominated by the volcano's nearly perfect cone.

Walk along Lake Villarrica and through Pucón's center. The town resembles an alpine resort, with its wooden houses and numerous adventure tour agencies. German settlers who arrived in the 19th century left their mark on local architecture and cuisine (kuchenes, cakes). Villarrica volcano (2,847 m), called RukaPillán (“the house of spirits” in Mapudungun), is one of South America's most active. Its last eruption was in 2015.

Ojos del Caburgua, two natural pools of turquoise water fed by waterfalls, nestled in the forest about 25 km from Pucón. The emerald water comes from underground rivers filtered through volcanic rock. The contrast between transparent water and dense vegetation creates a striking tableau.

Lake Caburgua, a lake with limpid waters surrounded by forests. Playa Blanca, a rare stretch of light sand in the region (sand is usually volcanic and dark), offers a swimming spot in summer. From the shores, views of snow-capped mountains plunging directly into the water.

Huerquehue National Park, 12,500 hectares of ancient forests 35 km from Pucón. The “Los Lagos” trail climbs through thousand-year-old araucarias - these prehistoric conifers are nicknamed “monkey puzzle trees” because their sharp needle-like leaves prevent climbing. The trail passes the Nido de Águila waterfall. Views of Villarrica volcano in the background.

activities.text: Settling in and free time at the end of the day. Walk on Lake Villarrica's beach with its gray volcanic sand. In good weather, the snow-capped volcano is reflected in the lake's calm waters.

Ascent of Villarrica volcano (2,847 m). Early morning departure from Pucón with mandatory guide. The ascent takes about 4 to 5 hours for 1,000 meters of elevation gain. The final meters cross the glacier capping the 200-meter-diameter crater - at the bottom, you can see magma. The volcano is an active stratovolcano capped by a 40 km² glacier. The descent partly involves sliding seated on the snow. Activity subject to weather conditions and volcanic alert level.

Hike on the Sendero Los Lagos in Huerquehue park, limited to the Nido de Águila sector currently accessible. The trail climbs through the forest and leads to the Nido de Águila waterfall. Return along the same path without continuing toward the Chico, Verde and El Toro lagoons while the access restriction remains in effect. Bring water and a picnic.

Thermal baths at the end of the day. Several thermal spas are tucked away in the mountain valleys around Pucón. Natural hot water, heated by volcanic activity, flows into stone or wooden pools surrounded by native forest.

days_plan.itin_title: Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers
Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers
Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers

visits.text: Isla Magdalena, 35 km northeast of Punta Arenas in the Strait of Magellan. This island of barely 1 km² shelters around 120,000 nesting Magellanic penguins. Designated as part of “Los Pingüinos” Natural Monument in 1982 along with neighboring Marta Island. The catamaran crossing takes 1 hour 30 minutes. On the island, a marked path winds between burrows dug in the ground. Each year between September and March, monogamous pairs return to nest in the same spot. Magellanic penguins measure 60 to 75 cm. The red and white lighthouse overlooking the island serves as a landmark for sailors in the strait.

Serrano Glacier, in Bernardo O'Higgins National Park, accessible by boat from Puerto Natales via Última Esperanza Fjord ("Last Hope Fjord," named by navigator Juan Ladrillero in 1557 after months searching for a passage to the Pacific). The glacier descends from the Southern Ice Field to a small lake. From the landing, a roughly 1 km trail leads to the glacier front.

activities.text: Boat trip in the Strait of Magellan (round trip to Isla Magdalena). During the crossing, you may see imperial cormorants, black-browed albatrosses, and sea lions on neighboring Isla Marta.

Drive Punta Arenas → Puerto Natales (about 3 hours, 250 km). The road crosses the Patagonian steppe, an immense grassy plain battered by wind. You regularly encounter herds of guanacos and sometimes rheas (South American cousins of the ostrich). Puerto Natales, a small town of 20,000 inhabitants on the shores of Última Esperanza Fjord, serves as the gateway to Torres del Paine park.

Boat trip on Última Esperanza Fjord. The boat follows cliffs where cormorants nest, passes waterfalls, and approaches Balmaceda Glacier (visible but not accessible on foot) before reaching Serrano Glacier. Vegetation shifts from steppe to subpolar forest as the fjord extends deeper into the mountain range.

Free evening in Puerto Natales. The town offers an end-of-the-world atmosphere with its houses clad in colorful sheet metal and restaurants serving Patagonian lamb slowly grilled over a wood fire (cordero al palo).

days_plan.itin_title: Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers
Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers

visits.text: Drive Pucón → Puerto Varas (about 4 hours 30 minutes, 315 km). The road crosses southern Chilean countryside between volcanoes and pastures. Stop in Frutillar Bajo, a German-speaking village on Lake Llanquihue's west shore. Founded by German settlers in the mid-19th century, Frutillar has preserved its half-timbered houses, flower gardens, and tea rooms serving kuchenes (traditional German cakes). The German Colonial Museum traces the history of this immigration. The Teatro del Lago, a concert hall on stilts facing the lake, hosts a classical music festival each summer.

Arrival in Puerto Varas, nicknamed the “City of Roses” for the rose gardens that bloom in every garden from December to March. This small town on the shore of Lake Llanquihue - the largest lake entirely within Chile - offers a direct view of the snow-covered cone of Osorno volcano (2,652 m), 50 km away on the other side of the lake. The colorful wooden architecture recalls the heritage of the German settlers who arrived here in the early 20th century.

Saltos del Petrohué, in Vicente Pérez Rosales National Park—Chile's first national park, created in 1926. The Petrohué River crashes through basaltic lava flows from Osorno volcano, forming rapids and turquoise waterfalls against black rock. The name “Petrohué” means “place of mists”, referring to the vapors produced when lava came into contact with water during past eruptions. In season, you can observe salmon swimming upstream.

Lago Todos los Santos, a lake of glacial origin with turquoise waters, surrounded by dense Valdivian forest. From the Petrohué pier, views of Osorno, Puntiagudo, and Tronador volcanoes. This lake is the starting point for the lake crossing to Argentina (Bariloche).

Scenic drive to Osorno volcano's ski center. The paved road climbs in switchbacks through forest to about 1,200 meters above sea level. From the viewpoints, views down over Lake Llanquihue on one side and Lake Todos los Santos on the other. Osorno volcano (2,652 m), a stratovolcano with a nearly perfect cone, has experienced eleven documented eruptions, the last in 1869.

Village of Ensenada, on Lake Llanquihue's east shore at the foot of Osorno volcano. This small rural hamlet serves as a starting point for visits to the national park's attractions. A few wooden lodges and local restaurants offer curanto (a traditional dish cooked underground) and lamb grilled on a stake (cordero al palo).

Ferry crossing of the Chacao Channel (about 30 minutes) to Chiloé Island. The island is known for its 16 wooden churches listed as UNESCO World Heritage, built by Jesuit missionaries in the 17th and 18th centuries using a technique that combines European craftsmanship and local materials - cypress and alerce wood, without a single nail.

Castro, capital of Chiloé founded in 1567—one of Chile's oldest cities. The palafitos, colorful houses built on stilts driven into the water, line Castro's fjord. Built by fishermen for direct sea access, they've become the island's symbol. San Francisco de Castro church, UNESCO-listed, stands out with its yellow and mauve facade and entirely wooden interior.

Dalcahue, a small fishing port 20 km from Castro. Its Sunday artisan market is renowned for Chilote wool, rush baskets, and seafood. Dalcahue's church, also UNESCO-listed, dominates the village square.

activities.text: Stroll along Puerto Varas' lakefront with views of Osorno and Calbuco volcanoes. The statue of Princess Licarayén, a figure from Huilliche mythology, recalls the local legend: she was allegedly sacrificed by her tribe to calm the evil spirit trapped in Osorno volcano, giving birth to the region's lakes.
Rafting on the Petrohué River amid temperate forest with Osorno volcano in the background. Class III rapids, accessible to beginners accompanied by a guide.

Tasting curanto, Chiloé's traditional dish cooked in a hole dug in the ground over hot stones, covered with nalca leaves. It combines seafood (mussels, clams), Chiloé potatoes (the island grows over 200 potato varieties), smoked meat, and chapaleles (flour cakes).
Return by ferry across the Chacao Channel, then drive to Puerto Varas/Puerto Montt (about 3 hours 30 minutes in total, including the crossing). Overnight in Puerto Varas.

days_plan.itin_title: Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers
Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers
Chile Road Trip: From the Atacama Desert to Patagonian Glaciers

places.name: Pukara De Quitor

visits.text: In the 12th century, the Atacameños built Pukará de Quitor on a promontory above the Río San Pedro. Around a hundred defensive enclosures cling to the slope. In 1540, the fortress resisted Pedro de Valdivia’s men before falling; it has been a national monument since 1982. The overlook closes at 6 p.m.

activities.text: You can reach Pukará de Quitor on foot or by bike: it is just 3.5 km from the center of San Pedro de Atacama, along the river. Climb to the top for a view over the entire oasis. Leave early to avoid the heat, and bring water.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

map_keywords: Pukará de Quitor San Pedro de Atacama

places.name: Punta Arenas

visits.text: Flight Puerto Montt → Punta Arenas (about 2 hours). Arrival in the southernmost city on the South American mainland, founded in 1848 on the shores of the Strait of Magellan. Before the Panama Canal opened in 1914, its port was a mandatory stopover for every ship connecting the Atlantic to the Pacific.

Plaza Muñoz Gamero, a central square shaded by cypress and birch trees. At its center stands a bronze statue of Ferdinand Magellan, the first European to sail through the strait in 1520. To the north of the square, Palacio Sara Braun, built in 1895 in a French neoclassical style over two floors, bears witness to the wealth of the great sheep ranchers of the 19th century.
Cerro de la Cruz, a viewpoint overlooking the city. On clear days, the view extends over Punta Arenas' colorful rooftops, the Strait of Magellan, and beyond to Argentine Tierra del Fuego.

Municipal Cemetery of Punta Arenas, established in 1894, ranked among the world's most beautiful cemeteries. Broad avenues lined with century-old cypresses, opulent mausoleums of ranching families enriched by wool and gold, and chapels made of Carrara marble imported from Italy. There is also the tomb of the Unknown Indian, a place of remembrance for the Indigenous peoples decimated after colonization—Selk'nam, Tehuelches, and Yaganes.

Nao Victoria Museum, a few kilometers from the center. Life-size replicas of four historic ships, including the Nao Victoria, the first vessel to complete a circumnavigation under the command of Magellan and then Elcano (1519–1522). The models give a sense of the cramped conditions aboard ships in the 16th century.

activities.text: Stroll along the waterfront by the Strait of Magellan. With luck, you might spot Commerson's dolphins offshore. The wind often blows hard - welcome to Patagonia.

map_keywords: Cerro de la Cruz Punta Arenas

visits.text: Built in 1670 to replace a church destroyed by an earthquake, the Iglesia de San Idelfonso de Putre retains an adobe nave and 19th-century restoration work. It is listed as a historic monument. Stop by toward the end of the day, when the square is quiet, with Taapaca volcano in the background.

A mountain stream cuts Avenida O’Higgins, the oldest part of Putre, in two. Behind modest facades, some houses have retained their carved stone entranceways and windowsills from the 17th century. The village sits at about 3,500 m: walk slowly, as this is your first day at altitude and you can quickly get out of breath.

activities.text: On Plaza de Putre, local custom calls for drinking mate de coca or mate de chachacoma, two herbal teas served hot. They are no substitute for acclimatization: drink plenty of water and avoid strenuous exertion on your first evening. One last crucial point: there are no gas stations in Putre or along the road to the park, so fill up in Arica.

The real agenda in Putre is to sit on Plaza de Putre and try a local dish such as picante de llaita. The stone and adobe houses set the tone for a peaceful village, something of a little San Pedro de Atacama without the crowds. Nights are cold: check that your accommodations have heating, as many basic guesthouses do not.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: In 2002, National Geographic named Quillagua the driest place on the planet. This Aymara village on the Río Loa now has only about 120 residents, down from more than 600 up until the mid-1970s. Services are very limited: arrive with water and a full tank of gas.

Chile’s longest river flows through the driest place in the world: the Río Loa, about 440 km long, runs below Quillagua. Its flow has dropped sharply, and according to Reporte Minero, seepage from mining waste ruined crops in the 1980s and 1990s. Take a short break in the shade of the carob trees before continuing to Calama.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

places.name: San Miguel De Azapa

visits.text: If the mummies caught your interest, head to the Museo Arqueológico San Miguel de Azapa, at kilometer 12 on the road through the Azapa Valley. It holds 15 Chinchorro mummies in a preservation room, along with a reconstruction of the mummification process and petroglyphs. These bodies are more than 7,000 years old, older than the Egyptian mummies. Set aside some time for the valley, known for its olives.

map_keywords: Museo Arqueológico San Miguel de Azapa Arica

places.name: San Pedro De Atacama

visits.text: Flight Santiago → Calama, then transfer to San Pedro de Atacama (about a 1-hour 30-minute drive, 100 km). The road crosses the Domeyko Range, a landscape of arid hills and ocher canyons. San Pedro sits at an altitude of 2,400 meters in the oasis of the same name, at the heart of the world's driest desert (outside polar regions).

Church of San Pedro de Atacama, considered Chile's second oldest. Built during the colonial period from adobe—unfired earth mixed with straw—it has a plain exterior and a cactus-wood ceiling (chañar and carob). A little gem of Andean vernacular architecture.

El Tatio geysers, the world's third-largest geothermal field and one of the highest on the planet, at about 4,280 meters above sea level. Leave before dawn (around 4 a.m.) to arrive at sunrise, when the freezing cold (down to -20°C) sends the most spectacular columns of steam shooting upward. The site has about 80 active geysers. Its name comes from the Kunza “Tata iu”—“the grandfather who cries”.

Village of Machuca, on the return road from the geysers. About twenty houses built from adobe and ichu grass, a small earthen church, and a single extended family making a living from llama herding. Residents sell grilled llama meat skewers to passing visitors.

Pukará de Quitor, a 12th-century pre-Inca fortress 3 km north of San Pedro. Built from liparite stone on an 80-meter promontory overlooking the San Pedro River, it served as a defensive position for the Atacameño people (Lickan Antay) against the Aymaras. In 1540, Francisco de Aguirre fought a decisive battle here: after his victory, he had the Atacameño chiefs and warriors beheaded—Spanish chronicles mention several hundred victims—and their heads were lined up on the walls, hence the nickname “el pueblo de las cabezas”. A National Monument since 1982. The summit viewpoint offers views over the oasis, the Valley of Death, and the Andes.

Aldea de Tulor, an archaeological site roughly 3,000 years old, among the oldest evidence of settled life in the Atacama Desert. The circular earthen foundations have been partially reconstructed to show the layout of the original Atacameño village. The site was discovered partly buried under sand.

Lagunas Miscanti and Miñiques, twin lagoons perched at around 4,200 meters above sea level on the altiplano. Their deep blue waters are framed by volcanoes of the same names. Vicuñas (protected wild cousins of the llama) often graze nearby. Absolute silence surrounds the lagoons, broken only by the wind.

Salar de Atacama, Chile's largest salt flat (roughly 3,000 km²). At Laguna Chaxa in the Los Flamencos National Reserve, observe three flamingo species - Chilean flamingo, Andean flamingo, and James's flamingo - filtering micro-algae from the brackish waters. Salt crystals form hexagonal patterns on the surface. This salt flat produces a significant portion of the world's lithium.

Village of Toconao, 38 km south of San Pedro. San Lucas church and its separate bell tower are built from locally quarried white volcanic stone (liparite). The village is surrounded by a verdant ravine where fig trees and quinoa grow.

Valle del Arcoíris (Rainbow Valley), about 90 km north of San Pedro. Mineral layers - iron, copper, sulfur, manganese - color the rock formations red, green, yellow, and violet. The site also features the Hierbas Buenas petroglyphs, carved by Atacameño caravaneers centuries ago.

activities.text: Valle de la Luna in late afternoon. This landscape sculpted by wind and erosion in the Salt Range evokes a lunar surface: sand dunes, salt ridges, and rock formations with multicolored strata. Sunset sets the minerals ablaze, transforming the terrain into a gradient of ocher, red, and violet. Bring warm clothes; the temperature drops rapidly after dusk.

Walk along the marked paths at El Tatio after watching the geysers at dawn. At an altitude of 4,300 m, fumaroles and geothermal flows can be viewed from the authorized paths. Stay on the trails without touching the hot water; the geothermal pool is not open for swimming.

Flamingo observation at Salar de Atacama. Three species coexist: Chilean flamingo (most common), Andean flamingo (endangered), and James's flamingo (rarest). Binoculars recommended to avoid disturbing the birds by approaching too close.

Nighttime stargazing. The Atacama Desert offers one of the planet's clearest skies—the world's largest observatories, including ALMA, are located here. Several operators offer sessions with telescopes and explanations of Southern Hemisphere constellations.

places.name: Santa Cruz Colchagua

visits.text: Valparaíso sits on 42 hills (cerros) above the port—UNESCO World Heritage since 2003. The city's identity is precisely this verticality: wood and corrugated iron houses painted in all colors, street art among the world's densest, and mechanical elevators ('ascensores') dating from the early 20th century. Cerro Concepción and Cerro Alegre concentrate the best of everything within walking distance.

Ascensor Concepción has operated since 1883—it's Chile's oldest still in service. The original cabin was replaced but the counterweight mechanism is intact. Ticket 300 CLP ($0.30), 60-meter journey. At the summit, Cerro Concepción spreads out with its alleys and views over Valparaíso Bay. Short but striking.

La Sebastiana, Pablo Neruda's third house (along with Isla Negra and La Chascona in Santiago), perches on Cerro Florida with a 270° bay view from the 5th floor. Neruda was a compulsive collector: ship models, salvaged stained glass, African masks, miniature bars installed in all his houses. The furniture remained as it was at his death in 1973. Allow 1 hour, ticket 9,000 CLP ($10). Closed Mondays.

Founded by Alexandra Marnier-Lapostolle—7th generation of the Grand Marnier family on the Chilean side—Lapostolle Clos Apalta is probably South America's most architecturally impressive winery. Six levels carved into the Apalta hillside, entirely gravity-flow cellar, and own-rooted vines over 100 years old (phylloxera never crossed the Andes). Clos Apalta, a blend of Carménère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Petit Verdot, was named Wine of the Year by Wine Spectator in 2008 for the 2005 vintage. Tour + tasting around $80.

Founded in 1988 by Aurelio Montes and three partners in an Apalta sector everyone deemed unworkable, the winery is organized according to feng shui principles—every angle, every corridor positioned accordingly. And since 1996, wines age in the cellar with continuous Gregorian chant music. Yes, really. Purple Angel (dense, deep Carménère), Folly (pure Syrah on the steepest slopes) and Montes Alpha M (Bordeaux blend) are the three cuvées to know. Tour + tasting $35-60.

The Museo de Colchagua in Santa Cruz is one of South America's richest private museums - created by industrialist Carlos Cardoen, a controversial figure, but the collection is astounding: pre-Columbian art, the colonial period, vintage cars. Open until 7 pm.

activities.text: Lunch at Caleta El Membrillo, by the fishing port: simple restaurants, fish grilled that morning, and chorrillana—fries covered with sautéed meat, eggs and melted onions, Valparaíso's popular dish that locals eat at all hours. Prices around $10-15 per person. It's loud, it's working-class, it's exactly what you need.

Afternoon drive to Santa Cruz: 3 hours via Ruta 5 South then Ruta I-50, flat terrain and road in good condition. Arrive early evening in Santa Cruz, capital of Colchagua Valley. The Plaza de Armas with its church and palms sets the tone: small town of 35,000 inhabitants, quiet, and entirely devoted to wine. Dinner possible at Los Varietales restaurant (Hotel Santa Cruz) or Vino Bello downtown.

Lunch at Viu Manent: a Chilean ranch-style estate, a 'huasos' atmosphere (Chilean cowboys), asados and empanadas cooked over embers in a breathtaking vineyard setting. Allow $35-50 per person. It is the most authentically Chilean place on the circuit—an open terrace, wood-fired beef, Carménère by the pitcher.

If the afternoon allows a third estate, Casa Silva in San Fernando is the most accessible option of the day: five generations of the same family, a polo field on site, and the Quintet (signature blend) to taste standing at the cellar. Low admission price, a no-fuss ranch atmosphere. Perfect for concluding a day already full of emotions. Plan a round trip from Santa Cruz for this visit to San Fernando.

Museo de Colchagua Santa Cruz Chile

visits.text: The Oficina Santa Laura preserves the industrial section: rusty machinery, a leaching plant and a large chimney visible from afar. Humberstone and Santa Laura have been jointly listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 15, 2005. Go there by car just after Humberstone, using the same ticket.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Plaza de Armas, Santiago's heart since Pedro de Valdivia founded the city on February 12, 1541. All distances in the country are measured from this square. At its center stands an allegory of Liberty in Carrara marble, sculpted by Francesco Orselino and unveiled in 1836, surrounded by around a hundred Chilean palm trees. There is also an equestrian statue of Pedro de Valdivia, donated by the Hispanic community for the 150th anniversary of independence. Chess players, mimes, and street dancers bring the square to life throughout the day.

Metropolitan Cathedral of Santiago, the fifth religious building on this site—the four predecessors were destroyed by earthquakes and fires. Construction of the current building began in 1748 under Bishop González Melgarejo. Architect Joaquín Toesca, who arrived in 1780, designed the neoclassical facade. The building was largely completed around 1830, then modified by architect Ignacio Cremonesi, who added the two towers and the Romano-Tuscan style. The interior is divided into three naves, with a marble main altar and a black-and-white mosaic floor. Beneath the floor, a crypt houses the tombs of Santiago's archbishops. Declared a National Monument in 1951, it hosts the ecumenical Te Deum every September 18 for Fiestas Patrias.

National History Museum, housed in the Palacio de la Real Audiencia on Plaza de Armas. Around 70,000 pieces trace Chile's story from pre-Columbian civilizations to the 1973 coup d'état. The final room displays Salvador Allende's broken glasses. Free admission.

Palacio de la Moneda, seat of Chile's presidency since 1845. Designed in 1784 by architect Joaquín Toesca, this neoclassical building originally served as the treasury where coins were minted. On September 11, 1973, it was bombed during the military coup. The building has since been restored, and the changing of the guard takes place every other day on the esplanade. The underground Palacio La Moneda cultural center hosts quality temporary exhibitions.

Cerro Santa Lucía, a 69-meter hill in the city center. The Mapuche used it as a lookout point before the Spanish arrived. Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago at the foot of this hill on February 12, 1541, using the promontory as a natural watchtower. The current park, redesigned in 1872 by mayor Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna, offers shaded walks, the Neptune fountain at the entrance, and a belvedere with views over the historic center.

Barrio Lastarria, an artistic quarter that developed around the Veracruz church, built in 1857, and was designated an Atypical Zone by the Ministry of Culture in 1997. Squeezed between Cerro Santa Lucía and Parque Forestal, it brings together the Museum of Fine Arts (opened in 1880), the Gabriela Mistral cultural center (built in 1972 for a UN conference), secondhand booksellers, and art galleries within a few streets. El Biógrafo cinema, opened in the 1980s, screens art-house films in a red velvet setting.

Mercado Central, Santiago's iconic covered market. The metal structure shelters stalls of fresh fish and seafood - congrio, locos, erizos - alongside numerous food stands. Step inside to taste caldillo de congrio, the fish soup Pablo Neruda celebrated in one of his poems.

Stop in the Casablanca Valley on the Santiago-Valparaíso road. This wine-growing valley, swept by Pacific mists, produces renowned whites—particularly sauvignon blanc and chardonnay. Several estates offer tastings.

Valparaíso, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003 for its 19th-century urban fabric adapted to the hills. The city sprawls across more than 40 cerros (hills) and once had up to 31 ascensores—funiculars built from 1883 onward to connect the lower city to the hills above. The first, Ascensor Concepción, dates to 1883. Seven remain operational. The port was the leading major port on the South Pacific route until the Panama Canal opened in 1914.

Cerros Alegre and Concepción, the UNESCO-listed historic heart. Cobblestone streets, houses with colorful facades, and architecture shaped by British and German immigrants in the second half of the 19th century. The Paseo Yugoslavo offers one of the finest panoramas over the bay. It can be reached via Ascensor El Peral, inaugurated in 1901, which connects Plaza de Justicia to Cerro Alegre. The Palacio Baburizza, built in 1916 on Cerro Alegre, houses the Municipal Museum of Fine Arts.

Plaza Sotomayor, the civic center of the lower city. At its center stands the Monument to the Heroes of Iquique, commemorating the 1879 naval battle during the War of the Pacific. The square is surrounded by the former Navy Command building and the historic customs house.

La Sebastiana, Pablo Neruda's house-museum perched on Cerro Bellavista. The poet installed his eclectic collections here: maritime objects, sculptures, paintings. From the garden viewpoint, panoramic views over the bay and Valparaíso's colorful rooftops.

Viña del Mar, a neighboring seaside resort nicknamed the “Ciudad Jardín”. The Flower Clock (Reloj de Flores), built in 1962, marks the entrance to the seafront. Stroll along Avenida Perú facing the Pacific.

Museum of Memory and Human Rights, opened to document the military dictatorship's violence (1973-1990). Exhibitions trace the stages of the September 11, 1973 coup d'état and its consequences. Testimonies, audiovisual archives, and victims' personal belongings. Free admission.

Chilean Museum of Pre-Columbian Art, housed in the Palacio Real Casa de Aduana (19th century) steps from Plaza de Armas. Ceramics, sculptures, textiles, and jewelry tell the story of pre-Columbian peoples from Mexico to Tierra del Fuego. The Chile room is particularly rich.

Maipo Valley, Santiago's main wine region, a 45-minute drive south. Vineyards stretch at the foot of the Andes. This valley produces mainly cabernet sauvignon, carménère (a grape that became Chile's emblem after disappearing from Europe following phylloxera), and merlot.
Transfer Puerto Natales → Punta Arenas (250 km, about a 3-hour drive), then flight Punta Arenas → Santiago (about 3 hours 30 minutes). Return to the capital for the final visits.

Sky Costanera, observation deck atop Gran Torre Santiago—South America's tallest skyscraper at 300 meters and 62 floors. 360° views over Santiago, the Andes, and, on clear days, the Coastal Range toward the Pacific. The contrast is striking after Patagonia's vast open spaces.

Free day in Santiago depending on departure flight schedule. Options: Parque Bicentenario in the Vitacura neighborhood (modern park with a flamingo lake), Providencia neighborhood for its cafes and bookstores, or a final visit to Mercado Central to bring back edible souvenirs (merken, Atacama salt, dulce de leche).

activities.text: Ascent of Cerro San Cristóbal by historic funicular, declared a Historic Monument in 2000. This 722-hectare park - Santiago's largest green space - peaks at 860 meters altitude. At the summit, a 14-meter statue of the Virgin of the Immaculate Conception (22m with pedestal) has dominated the city since 1908. Pope John Paul II celebrated mass here in 1987. On clear days, the view extends to Andean peaks exceeding 6,000 meters.

Stroll through Barrio Bellavista at the foot of Cerro San Cristóbal. Colorful facades, murals, and bohemian atmosphere. Visit La Chascona, one of poet Pablo Neruda's three house-museums, named for his wife Matilde's wild hair.
Wine tasting in the Casablanca Valley (stop on the Santiago-Valparaíso road)

Street art tour through Valparaíso's hills. The city's walls serve as a canvas for Chilean and international artists. The most spectacular murals are concentrated on Cerro Polanco and Cerro Bellavista, nicknamed the “open-air museum”.

Wine tasting in the Maipo Valley. Several wineries in the Pirque area offer cellar visits and tastings. Carménère, long confused with merlot, was rediscovered in Chile in the 1990s - it's now the country's signature grape.

Walk through Barrio Yungay, Santiago's historic working-class neighborhood. Plaza Yungay pays homage to the "Roto Chileno," the figure of the common soldier at the 1839 Battle of Yungay. Los Capuchinos church, built between 1853 and 1861 on a Florentine design, is worth the detour.

Stroll through Barrio Italia, a former Italian immigrant neighborhood transformed into an area of vintage shops, design workshops, galleries, and restaurants. Old houses with high ceilings now house creative businesses. A relaxed atmosphere on weekends, with flea markets in inner courtyards.
Final shopping and transfer to Arturo Merino Benítez International Airport for return flight.

visits.text: “Place of stones”: that is the meaning of the name Toconao, a village built from liparite, a volcanic rock that provides good insulation against the heat. The white bell tower, separate from the Iglesia de San Lucas, dates to 1750; both have been historic monuments since 1951. Artisans sell miniature bell towers carved from the same stone.

activities.text: If you have 1 hour, walk down into Quebrada de Jere, a green gorge that extends from the village of Toconao. Pear, fig, and apricot trees grow along the water, right in the desert. Bring water and a hat.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Chile in 13 Days, from Arica to the Atacama Desert

visits.text: Cueva del Milodón, a 30-meter-high, 200-meter-deep cave 24 km from Puerto Natales. In 1895, a piece of mylodon skin was discovered here - a giant herbivorous ground sloth 3 meters tall, extinct about 10,000 years ago. A life-size replica of the animal stands at the cave entrance. Traces of human occupation dating back 14,000 years have also been found here.

Entry into Torres del Paine National Park, established in 1959 and covering 181,000 hectares. Listed as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. The name “Paine” is said to come from the Tehuelche word “Payne”, meaning “blue” - the color found throughout the lakes and glaciers. The park borders the Southern Patagonian Ice Field.

Lago Pehoé, a lake with intense turquoise waters colored by "rock flour" - glacial sediments in suspension. From the shores, views of the Cuernos del Paine, two-toned peaks (black schist base, light granite summit) that evoke bull horns.

Salto Grande, a powerful waterfall between Lake Nordenskjöld and Lake Pehoé. A 4 km trail (round trip) leads from the parking lot to Mirador Cuernos, a viewpoint overlooking the Cuernos del Paine with Lake Nordenskjöld in the foreground. Allow 2 hours for the complete circuit.

Grey Glacier, a tongue of ice descending from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field into Lago Grey. The glacier measures about 6 km wide at its front and extends 28 km in length. Bluish icebergs regularly break off and drift on the lake. From the viewpoint accessible by a trail from Hotel Lago Grey (about a 1-hour 30-minute walk one way on gravelly terrain), you can make out the glacier's bluish mass at the far end of the lake.

The three Torres del Paine, granite columns that gave the park its name. Torre Sur (2,850 m), Torre Central (2,800 m), and Torre Norte (2,600 m) rise above a turquoise glacial lagoon. These towers are formed from intrusive granite 12 million years old, exposed by erosion of the softer schists that surrounded them.

Lago Nordenskjöld, a large elongated lake with blue-green waters, bordered by the base of the Cuernos del Paine. Named in honor of Finnish geographer and explorer Otto Nordenskjöld, who explored Patagonia in the late 19th century. In clear weather, the Cuernos are reflected in its waters. In December, the shores are covered with the red flowers of notro (ciruelillo), a shrub endemic to Patagonia.

activities.text: Wildlife observation in the park's steppe. Guanacos (wild camelids) are everywhere—the park reportedly has 3,000. Darwin's rheas, gray foxes, and, with plenty of luck, a puma. Andean condors patrol the sky, recognizable by their wingspan of more than 3 meters.

Boat trip on Lago Grey among the icebergs to the glacier front. The catamaran approaches within a few hundred meters of the ice wall. You hear the glacier cracking, and sometimes a block of ice breaks off with a dull crash. Light filters through the ice, creating shades of blue from turquoise to indigo.

Hike from Refugio Grey to Refugio Paine Grande (11 km). The trail follows the eastern slope of Cerro Olguín, with views of icebergs and the lake, crosses lenga forests (southern beeches) and then reaches the shores of Lake Pehoé. From Hotel Lago Grey, access to Refugio Grey is by boat; also arrange the catamaran crossing of Lake Pehoé to leave Paine Grande. This hike does not start from the beach at the southern end of Lago Grey.

Hike to Mirador Base Torres, Patagonia's most famous hike. About 22 km round trip with 850 meters of elevation gain; allow 8 to 10 hours. The trail climbs the Río Ascencio valley through lenga forests. The final section, called “the moraine”, is a steep ascent between boulders. The reward at the top: the turquoise lagoon at the foot of the three granite towers.

Hike in the Francés Valley (Valley of the French). Access involves crossing Lake Pehoé by catamaran and then walking to Campamento Italiano. From Campamento Italiano, climb through the lenga forest to Mirador Francés (about 4 hours round trip) or to Mirador Británico for the more ambitious (6 hours round trip), excluding the walk to the campsite and the lake crossing. The valley is hemmed in by the walls of the Paine Grande massif and the Cuernos. Hanging glaciers can be seen here, with pieces sometimes breaking off with a deep rumble.

places.name: Valle De La Luna

visits.text: Ocher sand, white salt crusts, and silence: Duna Mayor towers over Valle de la Luna, 13 km west of San Pedro de Atacama. A trail climbs onto its ridge, opening up views of the entire Cordillera de la Sal. Keep water with you; climbing through sand quickly wears you out.

Las Tres Marías, three rock formations sculpted by wind and erosion, have become the image of Valle de la Luna. Nearby lie the remains of Mina Victoria, a former mine. Do not touch the rocks; they are fragile.

Valle de la Luna is usually at its most beautiful at sunset from Mirador de Kari, also known as Piedra del Coyote. It has been closed until further notice since May 27, 2026, following a safety assessment after an earthquake. Check the official website to see whether it has reopened before booking a sunset tour.

Designated a nature sanctuary in 1982, Valle de la Luna is part of Reserva Nacional Los Flamencos and is managed jointly with Indigenous communities and CONAF. The route passes through the Anfiteatro, the Cañón, and a Cueva de Sal, where you walk among salt crystals. Buy your ticket online in advance; the recorded adult admission price was 10,800 pesos.

activities.text: You can enter Valle de la Luna by bike between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m., with a helmet, reflective vest, and water required. Pedestrians are not allowed on the park road. Leave San Pedro de Atacama early: cycling 13 km one way under the desert sun is already a substantial ride.
